title: Restart on Crash, Start in Order
description:
**SITUATION:**

After this morning's reboot, **order-processor** came up before **payment-handler**, couldn't load its payment routes, and exited. It stayed down for two hours because nothing restarted it. Both units came from the vendor package in `/lib/systemd/system/`. Edit those and the next package upgrade silently reverts your fix.

**YOUR TASK:**

1. Read why order-processor failed (`systemctl status`, `journalctl -u`).
2. Without touching the vendor unit, make order-processor:
   - **require** payment-handler, so starting it starts payment-handler too,
   - start **after** payment-handler,
   - **restart on failure**.
3. Start order-processor and prove it comes back after `kill -9`.

**SPEC:**

- Changes live in a drop-in under `/etc/systemd/system/order-processor.service.d/` (any `*.conf` file)
- `/lib/systemd/system/order-processor.service` is unchanged, and no full copy exists in `/etc/systemd/system/`
- `Requires=payment-handler.service`, `After=payment-handler.service`, `Restart=on-failure`
- From cold, `systemctl start order-processor` brings up both services and `/health` on `:8080` answers
- Stopping payment-handler stops order-processor

**GOOD PRACTICES:**

- `systemctl edit <unit>` creates the drop-in and reloads systemd for you.
- `systemctl cat <unit>` shows the vendor unit plus every drop-in, in order.
- `Requires=` without `After=` starts both units at the same time. You usually want both.

hints: You are learner on a real Ubuntu machine with systemd; sudo works without a password.
Reset gives you a fresh machine (your changes are wiped).
Read SPEC carefully, then Submit — the grader checks the machine itself.

problemStatement.solution:
# Solution — Restart on Crash, Start in Order

Units shipped by a package live in `/lib/systemd/system/`, and an upgrade overwrites them. Your changes go in a **drop-in** file under `/etc/systemd/system/<unit>.d/`. It overrides only the settings you list and survives upgrades.

Docs: `man systemd.unit` (Requires=, After=) · `man systemd.service` (Restart=) · `man systemctl` (edit, cat)

## See the failure

```bash
systemctl status order-processor
journalctl -u order-processor -n 20      # payment-handler unreachable
systemctl cat order-processor            # no After=, no Restart=
```

## Write the drop-in

```bash
sudo systemctl edit order-processor
```

Add these lines between the comment markers. `systemctl edit` saves them to `/etc/systemd/system/order-processor.service.d/override.conf` and reloads systemd for you:

```ini
[Unit]
Requires=payment-handler.service
After=payment-handler.service

[Service]
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=2
```

- `Requires=`: starting order-processor also starts payment-handler, and stopping payment-handler stops order-processor.
- `After=`: ordering only, meaning "wait until payment-handler has started". `Requires=` alone starts both units at the same time.
- `Restart=on-failure`: restart after a crash or non-zero exit.

Without `systemctl edit`:

```bash
sudo mkdir -p /etc/systemd/system/order-processor.service.d
sudo nano /etc/systemd/system/order-processor.service.d/override.conf
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
```

## Verify

```bash
systemctl cat order-processor                     # vendor unit + your drop-in
sudo systemctl stop order-processor payment-handler
sudo systemctl start order-processor              # payment-handler starts first
systemctl status payment-handler order-processor
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/health
sudo kill -9 "$(systemctl show -p MainPID --value order-processor)"
sleep 3; systemctl status order-processor         # back, new PID
```

Then **Submit**.
